question: Tell me about a time you led a technical decision that was unpopular with your team — how did you handle it?
answer: A couple of years ago I pushed to migrate our monolith's background job processing to a message-queue-based architecture, and most of the team was hesitant because it meant learning new operational tooling and touching a system that 'worked fine.' Instead of overriding the objection, I set up a short spike: I built a small proof of concept handling one real, painful job type, and presented it alongside the actual metrics we were fighting — timeout rates, retry storms, and the on-call pages they caused. I also asked the two most skeptical engineers to poke holes in it directly, which surfaced a legitimate concern about message ordering that I hadn't fully accounted for, and we solved it together before rolling out further. We agreed to migrate incrementally, one job type at a time, with a rollback plan for each. The unpopularity mostly came from uncertainty, not disagreement about the destination — once people could see and criticize a concrete implementation, buy-in followed. The lesson I took away is that a technical decision imposed by authority creates compliance, while one arrived at through a shared, falsifiable demonstration creates ownership.

question: How do you mentor junior developers?
answer: I start by understanding where someone actually is, not where their title suggests they should be — their first week I'll pair with them on a real ticket and watch how they approach debugging, reading unfamiliar code, and asking questions, which tells me far more than a resume does. From there I try to give them problems that are one notch harder than what they're fully comfortable with, with enough scaffolding that they can succeed but enough ambiguity that they have to make real decisions. In code review, I focus on explaining the 'why' behind a suggestion rather than just the 'what' — if I ask them to extract a function, I'll explain the testing or readability principle behind it so it generalizes to the next piece of code, not just this one. I also protect time for questions that feel 'too basic to ask in Slack' by having a standing weekly 1:1 that's explicitly for that. The clearest signal my mentoring is working isn't that they stop making mistakes — it's that the mistakes get more sophisticated over time, and that they start mentoring the next junior engineer themselves.

question: Describe a significant system design trade-off you made and why.
answer: When we built out our notifications system, the central trade-off was consistency versus availability under load. We could have made notification delivery transactionally tied to the triggering write — guaranteeing every event produces exactly one notification — but that would have coupled a high-throughput core write path to a slower, less reliable downstream system, and any notification-service hiccup would have started failing unrelated core operations. Instead, I chose an eventually-consistent design: the core write publishes an event to a queue, and the notification service consumes it asynchronously, with idempotency keys and at-least-once delivery semantics so a retried event never double-notifies a user. The trade-off was accepting a small, bounded delay (typically under a second) and the operational complexity of building idempotency handling, in exchange for the core system staying fast and resilient even if notifications backed up entirely. I made that call by mapping out failure modes explicitly — a slow notification service degrading the checkout flow was a much worse outcome for the business than a delayed push notification — and that ranking made the decision fairly clear once we'd written it down.

question: How do you handle disagreement with your manager or a peer on technical direction?
answer: My first move is to make sure I actually understand their reasoning before I push back — I'll ask what constraints or context are shaping their position, because disagreements are often about different information rather than different judgment. If, after that, I still think the direction is wrong, I lay out my concern in concrete terms: what specifically I think will break, under what conditions, and what it will cost to fix later versus now. I try to bring data or a small prototype rather than just opinion, since that keeps the conversation about the tradeoffs rather than about who's right. If we still disagree after that honest exchange, I follow a 'disagree and commit' approach — I'll say clearly that I still have reservations, make sure they're documented so we're not relitigating later, and then commit fully to executing the agreed direction rather than quietly dragging my feet. I've been on both sides of this: a case where I pushed back and we changed course, and a case where I was overruled and the decision turned out fine. Both outcomes reinforced that the goal isn't winning the argument, it's making sure the decision gets made with full information.

question: What's your approach to prioritizing technical debt against feature work?
answer: I treat technical debt the same way I'd treat any other backlog item — it needs to be visible, sized, and justified in terms of impact, not addressed through vague pleas to 'clean things up.' Concretely, when I identify debt, I try to tie it to a concrete cost: this area causes X hours of debugging per incident, or this coupling means every feature in this module takes 30% longer to ship safely. That lets it compete honestly against feature work in the same prioritization conversation, rather than being an afterthought squeezed in during slow weeks. I also try to bundle debt paydown with adjacent feature work when it's a natural fit — if a feature already requires touching a messy module, that's the moment to also fix the mess, because the cost of context-switching back into it later is much higher. For debt that's a genuine risk (security, a fragile system with no tests, a scaling ceiling we're approaching), I escalate it as a risk conversation with stakeholders rather than letting it silently compete with feature prioritization, because some debt isn't a 'someday' problem, it's closer to an outage waiting to happen.

question: How do you communicate technical risk to non-technical stakeholders?
answer: I translate the risk into business terms before I say anything technical — instead of 'our database doesn't have proper indexing on this query,' I'll say 'this page will get noticeably slower as we grow, and past a certain size it could start timing out for users during our busiest hours.' I try to always pair a risk with its likelihood, its blast radius, and the cost of addressing it now versus later, framed as a simple comparison a non-technical stakeholder can actually weigh — similar to how they'd think about an insurance decision. I avoid jargon entirely in these conversations and use concrete analogies or, when possible, a real number from production (response times, error rates, past incident costs) rather than abstract severity labels. I also make sure to state my actual recommendation, not just the risk — stakeholders don't want a technical dump, they want to know what I think we should do and why, and I leave room for them to ask questions or push back on the trade-off, since the business context they hold might change the right answer.

question: Tell me about a production incident you handled — what was your process?
answer: We had an incident where our checkout API's error rate spiked to about 15% during a traffic surge. My first step was to stabilize, not diagnose — I checked whether a recent deploy correlated with the spike and, since one had gone out 20 minutes earlier, we rolled it back immediately rather than trying to root-cause under pressure with users actively affected. That brought the error rate down within a couple of minutes, which bought us room to investigate properly. I then pulled logs and traces from the affected window, identified that the deploy had introduced a query that wasn't using an existing index under a specific filter combination, which caused connection pool exhaustion under load. We wrote up a timeline and root cause, added a regression test that would have caught the missing index, and added an alert on query latency percentiles so we'd catch a similar issue before it caused customer-facing errors next time. Throughout, I made sure to communicate status every 15 minutes in the incident channel even when there was nothing new to report, because I've learned that silence during an incident is more anxiety-inducing for stakeholders than 'still investigating, no change.' The postmortem was blameless by design — the goal was fixing the gap in our testing and monitoring, not assigning fault for a mistake anyone on the team could have made.

question: How do you approach reviewing a junior engineer's code without discouraging them?
answer: I separate feedback into what's blocking (a real bug, a security issue, something that will break in production) from what's a suggestion or preference, and I label it that way explicitly so they're not left guessing how seriously to take a comment. I lead with something genuinely specific I liked about the approach — not generic praise, but calling out a real decision they made well — because it signals I actually read the code carefully rather than just hunting for problems. For anything I ask them to change, I phrase it as a question or an explanation rather than a directive where possible: 'what happens here if the array is empty?' teaches them to find the bug themselves, which sticks better than me just naming it. I also try hard to distinguish 'this is wrong' from 'this is not how I would have written it' — junior engineers often internalize stylistic feedback as if it were correctness feedback, and over-correcting on style early can make them more hesitant and less creative in their solutions. If a review is going to have a lot of comments, I'll often do a quick call instead of a long comment thread, since tone is much easier to convey and tension much easier to defuse in a conversation than in text.
